plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two panels, (a) and (b), tracking ten fractional values through a bucket sort. Panel (a) is a vertical column of ten gray cells headed by the italic letter A, with row indices 1 through 10 running down its left side; from top to bottom the cells hold .78, .17, .39, .26, .72, .94, .21, .12, .23, and .68. Panel (b) is a second vertical column of ten gray cells headed B and indexed 0 through 9, each cell serving as the head of a linked list. The cells at indices 0, 4, 5, and 8 contain only a diagonal slash. The rest carry a horizontal arrow into a chain of two-field records, each record showing a value on the left and either a pointer arrow or a terminating slash on the right: index 1 leads to .12 then .17, index 2 to .21, .23, then .26, index 3 to .39 alone, index 6 to .68, index 7 to .72 then .78, and index 9 to .94. Each chain is in increasing order, and the leading digit of every value matches the index of the cell whose chain holds it, which is the correspondence the two columns invite the reader to check. The panels walk through distributing numbers drawn from the half-open interval from 0 to 1 into equal-width buckets, after which concatenating the sorted lists in index order gives the sorted output.

interactionPlan.concept: Bucket sort distributes values drawn from [0,1) into buckets whose index is floor(10·x), inserts each value into its bucket's linked list in sorted position, and concatenating the bucket lists in index order then yields fully sorted output.

ten gray cells in A holding, top to bottom: .78, .17, .39, .26, .72, .94, .21, .12, .23, .68
panel (b): vertical bucket array labeled 'B' (italic serif header) with bucket indices 0–9 along its left
empty-bucket marker: diagonal slash inside B[0], B[4], B[5], B[8] (NIL heads)
linked-list node boxes, each split into a value field (left) and a pointer field (right)
pointer field holds either a horizontal arrow to the next node or a terminating slash (NIL)

B[9] chain: .94 → NIL
horizontal arrow from each nonempty B cell's head into its chain's first node
sub-labels '(a)' and '(b)' beneath the two panels

api.does: returns the number of values in input array A
returns A[i], with indices running 1 to len() exactly as labeled in panel (a)
mathematical floor — enforces the half-open convention [i/10, (i+1)/10)
creates a node holding 'value' and splices it into B[bucket]'s linked list at its sorted position — the ONLY way to mutate B
records a learner comment shown on the current frame

interactions.frame: the full B column with its linked lists as built so far, the current A index being processed, and the node most recently inserted highlighted

input.label: Values in A (edit to test boundary cases like 0.05, 0.09, or 0.99)

interactions.sample_code:
for i in range(1, len() + 1):
    x = read(i)
    b = floor(10 * x)
    insertSorted(b, x)
interactions.buggy_code:
for i in range(1, len() + 1):
    x = read(i)
    b = round(10 * x)   # BUG: rounding misroutes values — .78 lands in bucket 8 instead of 7; bucket = floor(10*x)
    insertSorted(b, x)
interactions.success_check: every value x from A sits in bucket floor(10·x), and each nonempty bucket's linked list reads in ascending order
interactions.teaches: Routing each value into bucket floor(10·x) and splicing it into sorted position inside that bucket's list is the entire distribution step — get either part wrong and concatenating the buckets no longer yields sorted output

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Mapping x to bucket floor(10·x) means a bucket's index equals the leading digit of every value it holds, and because values are inserted in sorted position within each half-open bucket interval [i/10, (i+1)/10), simply concatenating the lists B[0] through B[9] produces the sorted output.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two panels side by side, matching the textbook figure. Panel (a): a single vertical column of ten gray-filled cells with the italic serif header 'A' above and row indices 1–10 listed to the left; values read top to bottom .78, .17, .39, .26, .72, .94, .21, .12, .23, .68. Panel (b): a second vertical column with header 'B' and indices 0–9 to the left; a nonempty cell's pointer field issues a horizontal arrow to a chain of two-field node boxes (value left, pointer right), pointers drawn as arrows or terminating slashes. Chains extend rightward and are laid out staggered so they don't overlap. Node chains must stay ascending left-to-right. Empty B cells show only a diagonal slash. The code-editor replay redraws this whole structure per frame — each recorded step highlights the current A index and the newly inserted node. Colors: gray cell fill with dark outlines and serif italic labels, matching the printed figure's style.

authoredContext:
Bucket sort assumes that the input is drawn from a uniform distribution and has an average-case running time of O.n/. Like counting sort, bucket sort is fast because it assumes something about the input. Whereas counting sort assumes that the input consists of integers in a small range, bucket sort assumes that the input is generated by a random process that distributes elements uniformly and independently over the interval Œ0; 1/. (See Section C.2 for a definition of uniform distribution.) Bucket sort divides the interval Œ0; 1/ into n equal-sized subintervals, or buckets, and then distributes the n input numbers into the buckets. Since the inputs are uniformly and independently distributed over Œ0; 1/, we do not expect many numbers to fall into each bucket. To produce the output, we simply sort the numbers in each bucket and then go through the buckets in order, listing the elements in each. Figure 8.4 shows the operation of bucket sort on an input array of 10 numbers.
To see that this algorithm works, consider two elements AŒi and AŒj . Assume
without loss of generality that AŒi _x0014_ AŒj . Since bnAŒic _x0014_ bnAŒj c, either
element AŒi goes into the same bucket as AŒj  or it goes into a bucket with a lower
index. If AŒi and AŒj  go into the same bucket, then the for loop of lines 7–8 puts
them into the proper order. If AŒi and AŒj  go into different buckets, then line 9
puts them into the proper order. Therefore, bucket sort works correctly.
To analyze the running time, observe that all lines except line 8 take O.n/ time
in the worst case. We need to analyze the total time taken by the n calls to insertion
sort in line 8
